title: Top 5 3D Product Collaboration Tools for Fashion Brands (2026)
content:
![](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202609/222821d8dcbb41789514725484482880/images/5c779710791d4f02a882b89513a450cftop-5-3d-collaboration-tools-thumbnail-1200sq.png)Ask a fashion team why they are looking at 3D collaboration tools and the answer is rarely about 3D alone. The challenge often appears when multiple teams and external partners need to review the same garment, follow revisions, and keep feedback connected to the correct product version.

3D collaboration platforms approach that problem in different ways. Some focus on fashion product development, some on collection collaboration, some on 3D asset management and distribution, and others on real-time CAD review.

This guide looks at five 3D product collaboration tools and the workflows each is designed to support.

## **TL;DR**

The five tools covered in this guide are:

  * **CLO-SET:** Fashion product development workspace combining browser-based 3D review, version management, product data, and Web Tech Pack workflows.

  * **Browzwear Stylezone:** Fashion collaboration platform for managing, reviewing, and merchandising collections within the Browzwear ecosystem.

  * **Style3D Cloud:** Cloud platform for managing, reviewing, and sharing digital fashion assets.

  * **VNTANA:** Enterprise digital asset management platform for managing, optimizing, governing, and distributing 3D and CAD product content.

  * **CADchat:** Browser-based collaboration environment for real-time and asynchronous review of CAD and 3D design files.




**The tools are presented by workflow focus, not ranked from best to worst.**

## **How We Compared These Tools**

Three questions structured this guide.

First, how does visual review work? Can teams and external collaborators inspect 3D assets in a browser and keep feedback connected to the product?

Second, what happens around the review? Does the platform support versions, product information, asset management, or other development context?

Third, who is the platform designed to connect? Some products are closely connected to a specific fashion design ecosystem, while others are designed to work across broader CAD, 3D, or downstream content workflows.

Feature descriptions in this article are based on each vendor's official website and published product documentation, reviewed in August 2026. Product capabilities and availability may change over time.

## **CLO-SET**

**Category:** Fashion product development and 3D collaboration workspace

CLO-SET is CLO Virtual Fashion's collaborative 3D creation workspace for fashion product development. It connects browser-based 3D review with product information, versions, comments and annotations, visual planning, and Web Tech Pack workflows in one centralized environment.

Teams can upload and manage 3D garment assets, review them through a browser-based viewer, and keep project files, versions, comments, and annotations connected to the same Content Page. External collaborators can review shared 3D assets without opening CLO.

CLO-SET also connects visual review with structured product information. BOM, measurements, construction details, cost information, and other product data can be managed alongside the 3D garment. Visual Board, Assortment, and other collaboration features extend the workflow into planning and merchandising.

For teams already developing garments in CLO, this creates a connected path from 3D design into review, product information, vendor collaboration, and production handoff.

Australian fashion group APG & Co, the company behind Saba, Sportscraft, and Jag, reported a **50% reduction in development and fit sampling costs in FY25** , with 100% of styles across the three brands developed and managed using CLO and CLO-SET. [Read the full APG & Co story](https://style.clo-set.com/en/resources/article/d15a2cda1cbe4398b2f2fa89601761e4).

**Key capabilities**

  * Browser-based 3D garment review

  * Comments and annotations connected to the 3D asset

  * Version history and review context

  * BOM, measurements, construction, and cost information

  * Web Tech Pack workflows

  * Visual planning and merchandising workflows

  * Role-based collaboration with internal teams and external partners




**Relevant for:** Fashion brands and vendors that want 3D garment review, product information, version context, and vendor collaboration connected within the same product-development workspace.

[**Sign Up Free**](https://style.clo-set.com/en/account/signup) to explore CLO-SET with the Free plan.

## **Browzwear Stylezone**

**Category:** Fashion collection collaboration platform

Stylezone is Browzwear's fashion collaboration platform for managing, reviewing, and merchandising collections.

According to Browzwear's official product materials, teams can synchronize VStitcher prototypes to the cloud, maintain a history of design updates and iterations, organize garment assets in a virtual design library, and manage comments and updates around styles.

Stylezone also supports work with colorways, trims, and materials in the cloud. Recent Browzwear updates have expanded its cloud-based creation and rendering capabilities while maintaining its connection with VStitcher and the broader Browzwear workflow.

**Key capabilities**

  * Cloud-based collection management

  * VStitcher prototype synchronization

  * Design update and iteration history

  * Comments and collaboration around styles

  * Colorway, trim, and material workflows

  * Collection and merchandising workflows




**Relevant for:** Teams using Browzwear that want cloud-based collection management, review, and merchandising around their 3D garment assets.

## **Style3D Cloud**

**Category:** Digital fashion asset management and collaboration platform

Style3D Cloud is Style3D's cloud platform for managing and sharing digital fashion assets.

According to Style3D's official product materials, the platform supports the storage, search, management, and presentation of digital fashion assets, including garments and materials. Teams can communicate design details online and use the platform to support collaboration across fashion product-development participants.

Style3D also describes Cloud as supporting collaboration among brands, suppliers, and manufacturers, with sharing options for presenting 3D styles to external recipients.

**Key capabilities**

  * Digital fashion asset storage and management

  * Search and organization of garment and material assets

  * Online review and sharing

  * Design-detail communication

  * Collaboration across brands, suppliers, and manufacturers

  * Presentation and sharing of 3D fashion assets




**Relevant for:** Teams evaluating Style3D Cloud for cloud-based management, review, and sharing of digital fashion assets.

## **VNTANA**

**Category:** Enterprise 3D and CAD digital asset management platform

VNTANA positions its platform as an enterprise digital asset management system for 3D, CAD, and other product content.

Its documented capabilities include centralized asset management, versioning, role-based access, automated CAD and 3D optimization, metadata management, review workflows, and connections to downstream systems such as PLM, PIM, eCommerce, and other content platforms.

VNTANA also supports preparing 3D and CAD assets for browser-based viewing and distribution across channels such as eCommerce, merchandising, sales, and AR experiences.

**Key capabilities**

  * Centralized 3D and CAD asset management

  * Version and metadata management

  * Role-based access

  * CAD and 3D optimization

  * Browser-ready 3D asset delivery

  * Connections to downstream product and commerce systems

  * Multi-channel 3D content distribution




**Relevant for:** Organizations managing large volumes of 3D and CAD product content that need centralized governance, optimization, and distribution across multiple systems and channels.

## **CADchat**

**Category:** Browser-based CAD and 3D review collaboration platform

CADchat is a browser-based collaboration platform designed around CAD and 3D model review.

Teams can open supported CAD and 3D files in a shared environment, inspect models, add comments and markups, and collaborate either during live meetings or asynchronously. CADchat supports a broad range of CAD formats and is designed for product-development and engineering workflows across industries.

Its focus differs from fashion-specific product-development platforms: the model itself serves as the shared context for review and discussion.

**Key capabilities**

  * Browser-based CAD and 3D model review

  * Live collaborative review sessions

  * Asynchronous design review

  * Comments and markups connected to the model

  * Support for multiple CAD and 3D formats

  * Persistent review workspaces




**Relevant for:** Cross-industry teams that need browser-based collaborative review of CAD and 3D design files.

## **How to Choose a 3D Product Collaboration Tool**

The right platform depends on where collaboration breaks down in your current workflow.

For fashion teams using CLO that want 3D review to stay connected with versions, product information, Web Tech Packs, and vendor collaboration, CLO-SET is designed around that workflow.

Teams working within Browzwear may consider Stylezone when collection review, asset organization, and merchandising need to stay connected with Browzwear garments.

Teams evaluating Style3D's product ecosystem can review Style3D Cloud for its documented capabilities around digital fashion asset management, sharing, and online collaboration.

Organizations whose primary challenge is managing, optimizing, governing, and distributing large libraries of 3D and CAD content across business systems may consider a 3D DAM such as VNTANA.

Teams whose main requirement is live or asynchronous collaborative review of CAD models across different industries may consider CADchat.

The important distinction is that these categories are not necessarily interchangeable. A fashion product-development workspace, a collection collaboration platform, a 3D DAM, and a CAD review tool can all work with 3D assets while supporting different parts of the workflow.

## **FAQ**

### **What is a 3D product collaboration tool?**

A 3D product collaboration tool provides a shared environment where teams can view, discuss, review, and manage work around 3D product assets.

In fashion, that often means keeping visual feedback and product-development context connected to a digital garment rather than relying only on exported files, screenshots, and separate communication channels.

Some platforms also connect 3D review with additional product information such as versions, specifications, BOMs, measurements, or tech packs. CLO-SET, for example, connects 3D garment review with [Web Tech Pack and product-development workflows](https://style.clo-set.com/en/solutions/brands).

### **What's the difference between a 3D collaboration tool and a PLM?**

PLM systems primarily manage structured product information and processes across the product lifecycle. A 3D collaboration platform focuses more directly on visual interaction with 3D assets and the review conversations around them.

The two categories can overlap, and their capabilities vary by vendor. Larger organizations may use both, with PLM acting as a broader system of record while a 3D collaboration workspace supports visual review and related product-development activities.

For a closer look at the different categories, see [**Do You Need a Fashion PLM? 8 Product Development Tools Compared**](https://style.clo-set.com/en/resources/article/d3a24e2976254e4ab816812436a4e780).

### **Can vendors and factories collaborate without installing 3D design software?**

All five platforms covered in this guide provide browser-based capabilities for viewing or collaborating around 3D or CAD assets. Exact account, licensing, permission, and external-access requirements vary by platform and plan.

CLO-SET allows shared 3D assets to be reviewed through its browser-based viewer without requiring collaborators to open CLO. Role-based access and sharing permissions can also be used to control which assets external partners can access.

### **Which tool is best for reviewing 3D garment samples?**

The appropriate tool depends on what needs to happen after the visual review.

When teams only need to inspect and discuss a model, a dedicated review environment may be sufficient. When review decisions also need to stay connected with versions, product specifications, measurements, BOM information, or vendor communication, a fashion product-development workspace may be more suitable.

For a step-by-step look at this workflow, see [**Digital Sample Review and Approval: A Complete Workflow for Fashion Teams**](https://style.clo-set.com/en/resources/article/83bcf55202f24384b7e226f9894d1b9b).

### **Do these tools replace 3D design software?**

Not necessarily.

These platforms connect to 3D creation workflows in different ways. Some are closely integrated with specific fashion design ecosystems, while others focus on asset management, review, or distribution across multiple CAD and 3D formats.

The 3D design software remains the authoring environment, while the collaboration layer supports activities such as asset management, review, communication, version context, and downstream product-development workflows.

* * *

Design reviews, version context, product information, and vendor collaboration connected around the same 3D garment — that's the workflow CLO-SET is designed to support.

title: 3D Sample Review vs Physical Sample Rounds: Cost, Lead Time, and When You Still Need the Real Thing
content:
![](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202608/0c19894871744193a1e2d4c62760dc4f/images/6e81feac233e4b348f0d8507c27ec1e73d-vs-physical-sample-rounds-thumbnail-1200.png)The pitch for 3D sampling usually overshoots. Somebody demos a garment rotating in a browser and the conclusion lands as “we can stop making samples,” which isn’t true and sets the project up to be judged against a promise it can’t keep. The defensible version of the argument is narrower: some of your sample rounds exist to answer questions that don’t require fabric. Those are the rounds 3D takes, and they’re where most of the iteration, and most of the waste, lives.

## **TL;DR**

3D and physical sample rounds answer different questions, and the economics favor replacing the early rounds, not the final ones.

  * A 3D sample review evaluates a simulated garment in a browser, covering proportion, styling, colorway, graphic placement, and fit direction, in hours and at no per-round material or freight cost.

  * A physical sample round evaluates the made garment and is the only way to judge hand feel, drape in an unfamiliar fabric, true color on a real substrate, wash and wear performance, and factory manufacturability.

  * Most teams settle on a hybrid: review proto and fit questions in 3D, then keep a physical pre-production sample before releasing bulk. Push 3D into the PP round and the whole program loses credibility.

  * The constraint on 3D accuracy is fabric data, not garment software. On a measured material, simulated drape is reliable, and entering the real fabric type, composition, and weight gets a new material close enough for direction-level calls. The final drape judgment on a fabric you've never run still belongs to the physical sample.

  * Fund a digitized fabric library and validated blocks before buying more authoring seats, and give reviewers browser access instead of licenses. Baseline four metrics before you change anything: physical rounds per style, days per review round, sampling spend per style, and the share of styles reaching pre-production without an extra physical round.

  * APG & Co, the Australian group behind Saba, Sportscraft and Jag, reported a **50% reduction in development and fit sampling costs** and an **80% time reduction on print strike-offs** in FY25 on CLO and CLO-SET, in the eighth year of an adoption that began in 2019.




## **What Is a 3D Sample Review?**

A 3D sample review is a review round run on a simulated garment instead of a sewn one. The team opens the 3D garment in a browser, checks proportion, colorway, graphic placement, and fit direction, and records comments and a decision against that version, in hours instead of weeks.

A physical sample round is the same decision process run on a made garment, and it answers a different class of question: how the fabric feels and falls, how color reads on the real substrate, and whether the factory can actually build the garment. Neither replaces the other outright. 

## **The Comparison, Side by Side**

![02321a0ba29b4d5ba2a3b0ca2df357d8](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202608/0c19894871744193a1e2d4c62760dc4f/images/02321a0ba29b4d5ba2a3b0ca2df357d8image.png)

**Time to produce.** A 3D review takes hours to a day, once blocks and materials are digitized. A physical round typically takes one to three weeks including make and freight.

**Marginal cost per iteration.** Effectively zero in 3D. Materials, labor, courier, and duties, every round, for physical.

**How many iterations you can absorb.** Many in 3D, because revising a colorway is a change, not a remake. Few physically, because each round consumes calendar.

**Who can participate.** Anyone with a browser link in 3D. Physically, whoever is holding the garment.

**Simultaneous review across regions.** Yes in 3D. Physically, no, unless you make duplicate samples.

**Proportion and styling.** Both answer this well.

**Colorway and graphic placement.** 3D answers this well. Physical answers it definitively.

**Fit direction.** 3D answers this well on digitized fabrics with validated blocks. Physical answers it definitively.

**Hand feel.** 3D cannot answer this. Physical can.

**Drape in an unfamiliar fabric.** 3D answers this reliably on a measured fabric, and approximately from the entered composition and weight. Physical answers it definitively.

**True color on the substrate.** 3D cannot answer this, because screen color is not a color standard. Physical can.

**Wash, shrinkage, and wear performance.** 3D cannot answer this. Physical can.

**Factory manufacturability.** 3D cannot answer this. Physical can.

**An audit record of the review.** 3D leaves one natively. A physical round leaves one only if somebody maintains it.

## **What a 3D Sample Review Answers Well**

**Proportion and silhouette.** Hem length, sleeve break, pocket scale, collar size, the relationship between panels. These are visual judgments, and a simulated garment on a correctly sized avatar answers them as well as a photograph of a real one.

**Colorway and print placement.** Applying six colorways to a garment in 3D takes minutes. Making six is a sample round. This is the single biggest source of physical rounds that 3D removes outright, and it’s where APG & Co reported their largest gain: an 80% time reduction on print strike-offs, achieved by finalizing prints, colors, and placement digitally before anything was printed.

**Graphic scale and position.** Where a logo lands relative to a seam, how a placement print reads across a size range, whether a graphic collides with a pocket. Cheap to check, expensive to discover on a physical sample.

**Fit direction.** With a validated block and a properly digitized fabric, 3D will tell you whether an armhole is fighting the sleeve or whether a waist seam is sitting wrong. It won’t replace a fit session, but it moves the conversation forward by a round.

**Review logistics.** A link opens for everyone at once. No duplicate samples for the buying team, no courier to the overseas merchandiser, no waiting on the one person holding the garment. This is also what makes supplier participation practical at scale: APG & Co onboarded 10 supplier factories onto the platform by 2025, covering half the group’s woven factories, and initially covered their license fees to remove the cost barrier.

## **What Only a Physical Sample Can Answer**

**Hand feel.** No simulation conveys it, and for a lot of product categories it’s a purchase driver.

**Drape in a fabric you haven’t used before.** Simulation quality tracks the fabric data behind it. A measured, previously validated material simulates reliably, and entering the real specs, meaning fabric type, composition, and weight, gets close enough for direction-level judgments, which is exactly what CLOFAB computes drape from. What stays physical is the final confirmation: that a fabric you’ve never run behaves on the garment the way its digital version says it does. ([This is why fabric digitization quality is the constraint on 3D accuracy, not the garment software.](https://style.clo-set.com/en/resources/article/3de990f60a4142f89d89c71343351c6d))

**True color.** Screens are not color standards. Lab dips and strike-offs get approved physically, under controlled light, against a physical reference.

**Wash, shrinkage, and wear performance.** Requires a real garment and a real machine.

**Manufacturability.** Whether a specific factory can build this garment repeatably, at quality, in bulk materials, is a question about the factory. That’s the pre-production sample’s job and 3D doesn’t touch it. See [pre-production sample review](https://style.clo-set.com/en/resources/article/44a6a3c0c8654d4ea7aa50babd20e59a).

## **The Hybrid Model Most Teams Land On**

![3500100bbf05461a8ae44899df47c636](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202608/0c19894871744193a1e2d4c62760dc4f/images/3500100bbf05461a8ae44899df47c636image.png)

  * **Concept and range review: 3D.** Decides which styles proceed, and whether the range hangs together.

  * **Proto: 3D,** with a physical sample only for construction you haven't built before. Decides silhouette, proportion, and construction approach.

  * **Colorway and graphic approval: both.** 3D for placement and scale, a physical lab dip or strike-off for the color itself.

  * **Fit: 3D pre-review, then one physical fit sample.** 3D resolves fit direction and the physical sample confirms it.

  * **Pre-production: physical, always.** Decides factory manufacturability and releases bulk.

  * **TOP or shipping: physical.** Decides whether bulk output matches the approved PP sample.




The pattern: 3D compresses the front of the calendar, where iteration is cheap and questions are visual. Physical samples hold the back of the calendar, where the decisions are about materials and manufacturing. Teams that try to push 3D into the PP round usually end up discrediting the whole program.

## **What It Costs to Set Up**

The per-round savings are real, and they’re preceded by fixed work that belongs in the business case.

  * **Digitized fabric library.** The largest and most valuable investment. Accuracy downstream depends on it, and it compounds, because a validated material gets reused across every style that follows.

  * **Validated blocks and avatars.** 3D fit judgment is only trustworthy against blocks that have been checked against real garments.

  * **Asset organization.** A 3D program generates files quickly, and unmanaged files stall reviews as effectively as slow sampling does. Worth solving before scaling: [how to manage and share 3D garment files](https://style.clo-set.com/en/resources/article/e4676767464541a5b94f57e11082ee2c).

  * **Reviewer access, not reviewer licenses.** The common budgeting mistake is pricing a 3D seat for everyone who needs to look at a garment. Reviewers need to view and comment, which a browser-based viewer covers. Only the people building garments need authoring software.

  * **Time for the workflow to settle.** APG & Co’s figures come from an adoption that started in 2019, not from a quarter. Their own sequencing is worth borrowing: Saba reached 100% of development styles on CLO in 2022, Sportscraft and Jag followed in 2023, and the ten supplier factories were onboarded by 2025. The early gains are logistical, meaning faster reviews and faster strike-offs. The larger cost reductions arrived once supply-chain adoption crossed critical mass.




## **How to Tell Whether It’s Working**

![b619da6ed49b4a818a3f760278fcbc0b](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202608/0c19894871744193a1e2d4c62760dc4f/images/b619da6ed49b4a818a3f760278fcbc0bimage.png)

Four metrics, tracked per season rather than per style:

**1\. Physical rounds per style.** The headline number. If 3D is working, this falls.

**2\. Days per review round.** Should drop immediately, since it’s mostly logistics.

**3\. Sampling spend per style.** Materials, labor, freight, duties. The number a CFO will ask for.

**4\. Share of styles reaching PP without an extra physical round.** The cleanest signal that 3D decisions are holding up.

Baseline all four before you change anything. A 3D program without a pre-change baseline is very hard to defend at budget time, which is the most common reason good programs get cut.

## **How CLO-SET Handles This**

CLO-SET is the workspace where the hybrid model runs. 3D garments, sample photography, digitized fabrics, and the tech pack live on the same Style inside shared Rooms.

Every 3D file gets a browser-based 3D Viewer, so merchandisers, buyers, and factories review garments without a CLO license. That is the reason 3D review gets cheap enough to use on every round, not only on hero styles. Rounds arrive as new versions of the same Style, pushed in from CLO with Direct Upload. Feedback splits into Annotation for notes pinned to a point on the garment and Comment for threaded discussion. Decisions are recorded by changing the style’s Workflow Status, with a separate Status on each colorway, and both sets of names are defined per company. Assortment gives the range-level view for deciding on multiple Styles at once. Access is set with Permission at Space, Room, or Style level. Fabrics can be digitized in-house with CLOFAB, and the materials side is where CLO Virtual Fashion is investing hardest: the company acquired [swatchbook](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/clo-virtual-fashion-acquires-swatchbook-solidifying-leadership-in-digital-fabric-solutions-302494231.html), the digital materials platform, in 2025, folding it into its materials division. Since fabric data is the constraint on 3D accuracy, that is exactly where the investment belongs. And because garment data is structured, Measurement and Bill of Materials feed the specification from the same Style the review ran on.

APG & Co’s FY25 results, reported by the Australian trade publication Ragtrader, are the clearest picture of what the hybrid model delivers at group scale:

Development and fit sampling costs: down 50%.

Print strike-off time: down 80%.

Styles developed and managed on CLO and CLO-SET: 100%, across Saba, Sportscraft and Jag.

Supplier factories onboarded: 10, covering half the group’s woven factories.

First CLO adoption: 2019, as the first Australian fashion retailer to do so.

Read those figures as a result of CLO and CLO-SET together. Designing in 3D removes the guesswork from the garment. It does not remove the email thread, the couriered strike-off, or the question of which version the factory is holding. Those go away when review, versioning, and approval run in a shared workspace as well, which is where the supply-chain-wide part of the saving comes from.

The figures were also assessed externally: the group was named a Best Use of Technology finalist at the 2026 AFIA on the strength of that work.

[Read the full story](https://style.clo-set.com/en/resources/article/d15a2cda1cbe4398b2f2fa89601761e4), or the underlying report in [Ragtrader](https://www.ragtrader.com.au/news/afia-finalists-2026-best-use-of-technology).

**[**[**Try CLO-SET for free**](https://style.clo-set.com/aboutus)**]**

## **FAQ**

**Can 3D sampling replace physical samples entirely?**

No, and programs sold on that premise tend to fail. 3D replaces the rounds that answer visual questions: proportion, colorway, graphic placement, fit direction. Hand feel, true color, wash performance, and factory manufacturability need a physical garment. The realistic target is fewer physical rounds, with a pre-production sample retained before bulk. That said, teams with years of accumulated experience and a deeply digitized asset base do push further: on repeat styles running at validated factories in already-approved materials, some go all the way to bulk with no physical round at all. That is an end state earned through validation, not a starting point.

**How much does 3D sampling actually save?**

It depends on how many of your current rounds are visual-question rounds, which varies a lot by category. As a published reference point, APG & Co reported a 50% reduction in development and fit 스sampling costs and an 80% time reduction on print strike-offs in FY25, in the eighth year of an adoption that began in 2019. The most reliable way to forecast your own number is to count how many of last season’s rounds were resolved by looking rather than touching.

**Is 3D fit accurate enough to approve a fit?**

It’s accurate enough to make fit decisions when the block has been validated against real garments and the fabric data is real: measured with a fabric kit, or at minimum entered from the actual type, composition, and weight rather than guessed. Both conditions matter. On a fabric you’ve never run, most teams use 3D to resolve fit direction and keep one physical fit sample to confirm.

**Do reviewers need 3D software licenses?**

No, on a platform with a browser-based viewer. Reviewers rotate, zoom, and comment on the garment through a link, in any browser, without installing anything. Only the people authoring garments need 3D software, which is also why external factories and buyers can be included without seat cost.

**What’s the first thing to invest in when starting 3D sampling?**

Fabric digitization. Every downstream claim about 3D accuracy rests on material data, and it’s the asset that compounds across seasons. Validated blocks come second. Buying more authoring seats before either of those is the usual way a program stalls.

**Should we still do a pre-production sample if the 3D review was approved?**

Yes. A 3D review can’t evaluate whether a specific factory can build the garment repeatably in bulk materials, which is the only thing a PP sample exists to establish. Skipping it means the first bulk-materials, bulk-line garment you see is the production run.

The silhouette was settled at proto. The fit was settled two rounds ago. What’s left is the dullest and most expensive question in the whole calendar: can this factory, on this line, with these materials, make this garment correctly, over and over? Approve it and bulk fabric gets cut. Approve it carelessly and you find out at TOP, when there is no round left to fix anything.

## **TL;DR**

A pre-production sample, usually shortened to PP sample, is the last sample made before bulk production, and the PP review is the round that decides whether bulk fabric gets cut.

  * It must be sewn by the factory that will produce the order, on their equipment, in the approved bulk fabric and trims. A well-made sample from any other facility answers a different question.

  * Design and fit are locked by this point, so the round is not a design review. It answers one question: is this garment correctly and repeatably manufacturable here, to spec?

  * The review checks five things: construction against the tech pack, measurements against the graded spec at tolerance, approved materials, labeling and compliance, and workmanship. Measure before you judge how the garment looks, and record actuals rather than pass or fail.

  * Sign-off splits by function: the technical designer owns conformance to spec, QA owns quality acceptance, and production and sourcing own the release of bulk materials. The designer flags appearance deviations without re-opening design, and the factory never approves its own sample.

  * It closes with a written decision of approve, approve with conditions, or reject, recorded against a specific sample with one named owner. Distributed approval is how bulk gets cut on a garment nobody actually cleared.

  * Most of a PP review runs remotely. Conformance to the tech pack, measurement verification, labeling, workmanship inspection, and the decision record all work digitally. Drape and on-body behavior simulate reliably once the fabric's physical properties are measured. Hand feel, true color against a physical standard, and wash performance still need the physical garment.

  * Four of the five most common rejection causes are upstream review failures rather than factory failures, which is the argument for closing every earlier round with a recorded decision. Teams that run every round this way have numbers to show for it: APG & Co reported a **50% reduction in development and fit sampling costs** in FY25, running 100% of styles across three brands on CLO and CLO-SET.




## **What is a Pre-Production Sample?**

A pre-production sample is the garment the production factory sews on its own line, in the approved bulk fabric and trims, to prove it can manufacture the style to specification before bulk cutting is released.

That definition carries three requirements, and the review tests all of them. The right factory: the facility that will actually run the order, not a development sample room. The right materials: approved bulk fabric, lab dips, strike-offs, and trims. The right document: the current tech pack, with every correction from the earlier rounds written in. Remove any one of the three and the sample stops answering the question this round exists to ask.

## **Where the PP Sample Sits in the Sequence**

  * Proto, or first sample. Made by a sample room or development vendor, to confirm the concept, silhouette, and construction approach. Approving it means the style keeps developing.

  * Fit sample. Made by a sample room or vendor, to confirm base-size fit, balance, and measurements. Approving it locks the fit and the grade.

  * Pre-production sample, or PP sample. Made by the production factory, to confirm that factory can build to spec in bulk materials. Approving it releases bulk cutting.

  * TOP, or shipping sample. Made by the production line, to confirm bulk output matches the approved PP sample. Approving it releases the shipment.




The distinction that matters most: a fit sample can come from anywhere, including a sample room on the other side of the world from where the order will be made. A PP sample has to come from the actual production factory. That’s the entire point of the round. A beautifully executed sample from the wrong facility tells you nothing about the order you’re placing.

## **What a Pre-Production Sample Review Actually Checks**

The check breaks into five blocks, and reviewing them in this order stops the round from drifting into design commentary.

![e40dd15aa3294962a80e55bfffbc6c3a](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202608/44a6a3c0c8654d4ea7aa50babd20e59a/images/e40dd15aa3294962a80e55bfffbc6c3aimage.png)

**Construction against the tech pack.** Seam types, stitch density, topstitch placement and margin, seam finishes, interlining and fusing, pocket and closure construction, bar tacks and reinforcement points. The question is conformance, not preference: does it match the specification the factory was given?

**Measurements against the graded spec.** Measure the base size at every point of measure and confirm each is inside tolerance. Where the order includes size extremes, measure the largest and smallest as well, because grading problems surface at the ends of the range, not the middle. Record actuals, not pass or fail. A garment sitting at the edge of tolerance on four consecutive points is drifting, even though nothing failed.

**Materials.** Bulk fabric, not substitute. Approved lab dip and strike-off, not “close enough.” Trims, zippers, buttons, elastic, thread, all the approved articles from the approved suppliers. A PP sample sewn in substitute fabric is a fit sample wearing a PP label.

**Labeling and compliance.** Care and content labels, size labels, brand labels, country of origin, any market-specific regulatory marking, plus placement of each. This block gets skipped more often than any other and is the most expensive to discover late, because it can strand finished goods at a border.

**Workmanship and finishing.** Pressing, thread trimming, symmetry, print and graphic placement, hardware finish, overall appearance on the form. This is where you judge whether the factory’s output quality is what you’re selling.

## **Who Signs Off on a PP Sample**

  * Technical designer reviews measurements, construction conformance, and grading, and owns the decision on whether the garment meets spec.

  * Quality or QA reviews workmanship, finishing, defect risk, and compliance marking, and owns quality acceptance.

  * Production and sourcing reviews feasibility at volume, capacity implications, and cost impact, and owns the release of bulk materials.

  * Designer reviews appearance in the bulk fabric against the original intent, and owns flagging an appearance deviation. That is not a license to re-open design.

  * The factory raises anything that is unbuildable as specified, and owns no approval decision. A factory does not approve its own PP sample.




One person should hold the final release. Distributed approval is how bulk gets cut on a garment that three functions each assumed a fourth had cleared.

## **The PP Review, Step by Step**

**1\. Confirm the sample is eligible before you review it.** Correct factory, bulk materials, approved lab dips and strike-offs. If it fails eligibility, stop. Reviewing an ineligible sample produces comments that will have to be re-checked anyway.

**2\. Measure first, look second.** Once you’ve decided how the garment looks, measurement discipline suffers. Take the numbers cold, record actuals against the spec sheet, and only then put the garment on the form.

**3\. Review construction against the tech pack, side by side.** Work from memory and a changed seam finish slips through. If your specification is generated from the garment data itself, the two are far harder to drift apart. [Here’s how a tech pack can be generated directly from the 3D garment](https://style.clo-set.com/en/resources/article/4c680edb7dd0417fb49086d0e812a74a).

**4\. Photograph and pin every comment to the garment.** One issue per comment, and state the correction, not only the observation. “Left welt pocket 4 mm low, match right at 12 cm from CF” is closeable. “Pockets uneven” starts a new thread.

**5\. Record a single decision with an owner and a date.** Approved means release bulk. Approved with conditions means release bulk, with a listed set of corrections that must appear at TOP. Write that list somewhere structural, because conditions left in a comment stream are conditions nobody checks. Rejected means a second PP sample is required, and you should say what has to change and confirm the calendar impact in the same message.

![93804f41e3004486bb07411c57082591](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202608/44a6a3c0c8654d4ea7aa50babd20e59a/images/93804f41e3004486bb07411c57082591image.png)

**6\. Push every accepted correction into the tech pack, then close the round.** The factory works from the specification, not from your review notes. A correction that never reaches the spec is a correction that reappears at TOP. Update the spec first, change the workflow status second, so the record and the document agree.

## **Common Reasons PP Samples Get Rejected**

Most rejections trace to something upstream, not to the factory.

**Substitute materials.** The bulk fabric wasn’t ready, so the factory sewed in something similar to keep the calendar. Drape, weight, and shrinkage all shift, and the measurements come back out of tolerance for reasons that have nothing to do with the pattern.

**Spec drift.** The fit round produced corrections that were agreed in conversation and never written into the tech pack. The factory built what it was given.

**Grading problems at the size extremes.** The base size measures perfectly. The largest size doesn’t, because the grade rules were never validated past the middle of the range.

**Unresolved fit comments carried forward.** A fit round closed ambiguously, the open item was assumed handled, and it arrives unhandled with only one round left.

**Late compliance requirements.** A market-specific label or content requirement surfaces after the sample was made, and correcting it changes construction.

Four of those five are review-process failures, not manufacturing failures. That’s the argument for closing every earlier round with a recorded decision instead of a quiet thread. The full workflow is here: [digital sample review and approval](https://style.clo-set.com/en/resources/article/83bcf55202f24384b7e226f9894d1b9b).

## **Can You Run a PP Review Remotely?**

Partly, and the split is fairly clean.

![53562c4730c24eb09a228ef8b23974a8](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202608/44a6a3c0c8654d4ea7aa50babd20e59a/images/53562c4730c24eb09a228ef8b23974a8image.png)

**Works remotely:** construction conformance against the tech pack, measurement verification (with the factory measuring on a shared, structured sheet and photographing the tape in position), labeling and placement, print and graphic placement, workmanship inspection through detailed photography or video, and the entire comment and decision record.

**Doesn’t work remotely:** hand feel, true color against a physical standard, and wash performance, because shrinkage and twist after laundering come out of physical testing, not simulation.

**Drape and on-body behavior sit in between.** Both simulate reliably when the fabric’s physical properties are measured rather than estimated: accurately enough to make drape and fit calls on screen, with fit, stress, and strain maps showing where a garment pulls or strains on the body. What the physical PP sample adds is confirmation that the actual bulk fabric behaves the way its digitized version predicted.

The practical arrangement most teams land on: the physical PP sample stays at the factory and a duplicate ships to the brand, while the review itself, meaning comments, measurements, and decision, runs digitally so every participant is looking at the same record. That way the round doesn’t wait on a courier, and the approval history exists somewhere other than an inbox.

## **How CLO-SET Handles This**

CLO-SET gives the PP round a single place to live. Sample photography, measurement records, reference 3D garments, and the tech pack sit together on the same Style inside a shared Room.

Each round arrives as a new version of that Style instead of another file, so a comment stays bound to the sample it described. Feedback splits into Annotation for notes pinned to a point on the garment, exportable to PDF so the factory gets the markup alongside the spec, and Comment for threaded discussion with attachments. The decision is recorded by changing the style’s Workflow Status, using stage names each company defines in Company Settings, so “PP approved” means the same thing to everyone. Each colorway carries its own Status alongside it. Vendor access is set with Permission at Space, Room, or Style level, so the factory participates without a CLO license and without receiving your editable files. Measurement tracks 2D and 3D measurements against target measurements, which is the part of a PP review that most often gets retyped into a spreadsheet, and the Web Tech Pack (BOM, POM, Construction, and Cost Estimation) carries the spec through the production stages so accepted corrections reach the document the factory actually works from.

The materials question doesn’t have to wait for a courier either. With [CLOFAB](https://style.clo-set.com/en/resources/article/3de990f60a4142f89d89c71343351c6d), the fabric digitization tool built into CLO-SET, a supplier can digitize the actual bulk fabric before the PP sample is sewn: scan a swatch with the CLO zFab Kit, or start from a fabric image where there’s no hardware on site, then enter the composition, weight, and thickness and the drape is computed from the specs. It runs in the browser with no CLO license and no installation, which keeps the barrier low for suppliers still new to 3D. The digitized fabric lands in the Workroom or Company Library, so the 3D garment the team reviews ahead of the PP round is wearing the fabric the order will actually use. Hand feel and true color still belong to the physical sample. What moves earlier is everything fabric-driven that can be judged by eye: drape direction, weight behavior, and how the approved material sits on the garment.

The effect tends to show up as fewer rounds rather than faster ones. APG & Co, the Australian group behind Saba, Sportscraft and Jag, reported a 50% reduction in development and fit sampling costs in FY25, with 100% of styles across the three brands managed on CLO and CLO-SET and 10 supplier factories onboarded. Their framing of what changed is the useful part for a PP round: physical samples became confirmations rather than experiments. Those results were assessed externally, earning the group a Best Use of Technology finalist place at the 2026 Australian Fashion Industry Awards. [Read the full story](https://style.clo-set.com/en/resources/article/d15a2cda1cbe4398b2f2fa89601761e4).

**[**[**Try CLO-SET for free**](https://style.clo-set.com/aboutus)**]**

## **FAQ**

**What is the difference between a fit sample and a pre-production sample?**

A fit sample tests the pattern, covering base-size measurements, balance, and how the garment sits on body, and it can be made by any competent sample room. A pre-production sample tests the factory: it must be sewn by the facility that will produce the order, using approved bulk fabric and trims, to prove the garment is manufacturable to spec there. Fit is a pattern question. PP is a manufacturing question.

**What is the difference between a PP sample and a TOP sample?**  
A PP sample is sewn before bulk production starts, to prove the factory can build the garment to spec in bulk materials, and approving it releases bulk cutting. A TOP sample, or top of production, is pulled from the bulk run itself, to confirm production output matches the approved PP sample, and approving it releases shipment. PP asks whether production may start. TOP asks whether what was produced matches what was approved.

**How long does pre-production sample approval usually take?**

The review itself is short, a few hours of technical work. The calendar cost is in the loop around it: waiting for bulk materials, shipping the sample, collecting comments from several functions, and returning a consolidated decision. Teams that shorten PP approval do it by compressing the feedback loop, not the inspection, which is why the round is a common candidate for digital review.

**Can you skip the pre-production sample?**

Occasionally, on a repeat carryover style at a factory with an established quality record and no material changes. On anything new, whether that’s a new style, factory, fabric, or construction, skipping it means the first bulk-materials, bulk-line garment you see is the production run itself. The saved week is generally cheaper than the rework it risks.

**What does “approved with conditions” mean on a PP sample?**

It means bulk is released, but named corrections must be present at TOP. It only works if the conditions are recorded somewhere structural, with an owner, and actually checked at the next round. Conditions left inside a comment thread are the most common way a known defect reaches production.

**Does a PP sample need to be in final packaging with final labels?**

Labels yes. Care, content, size, brand, and origin marking should all be present and correctly placed, since labeling errors are expensive to discover after goods are finished. Packaging is usually verified separately, often at TOP, but confirm which your buyer or market requires rather than assuming.

**Who is responsible if bulk is cut against a PP sample that was wrong?**

Contractually it depends on the terms. Practically it depends on the record: which sample was reviewed, what was decided, who decided it, and whether the corrections reached the tech pack. Disputes are settled by that record, which is the strongest argument for keeping version history and decisions in one system rather than reconstructing them from email.

title: Digital Sample Review and Approval: A Complete Workflow for Fashion Teams
content:
![](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202608/83bcf55202f24384b7e226f9894d1b9b/images/17bc023db7894b0c8f95d8bac83cf1aadigital-sample-review-thumbnail-1200.png)![](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202608/83bcf55202f24384b7e226f9894d1b9b/images/88b9a1c29ef34f0eb11aa54fdff8b17bdigital-sample-review-thumbnail-600.jpg)A fit sample lands on the desk. Someone photographs it against a white wall, drops four images into an email, and writes "shoulder looks off." Three days later the vendor replies asking which shoulder, the merchandiser has forwarded an older photo to the buyer, and the pattern maker is holding a correction nobody approved. Nobody was careless. The review had nowhere to live.

## **TL;DR**

A digital sample review is a structured round in which a sample, either 3D or photographed physical, is reviewed inside one shared workspace, with comments pinned to the garment itself, version history tracked automatically, and a recorded decision of approve, revise, or reject.

  * The workflow has six steps: name the round and what it decides, upload each round as a new version of the same style, pin feedback to the exact point on the garment, change the workflow status explicitly when a decision is made, update the tech pack on every round, and close the round before either opening the next version or releasing the style.

  * Email is the wrong container because a sample review produces four things at once: spatially anchored feedback, a version, a decision, and an audit record. Email carries the first one badly and the other three not at all.

  * Assign decision rights by function rather than shortening the invite list, and give every round one named decision owner. The most expensive failure in sampling is two functions each believing the other approved something.

  * Three physical rounds is the common baseline for a style with no unusual construction: proto, fit, and pre-production. Teams that pre-review in 3D routinely recover one of them, because proportion, colorway, and graphic placement get settled before anything is cut.

  * Judge sample review software on four things: a browser-based viewer that needs no license, comments pinned to the asset, versioning that lives on the record and not in file names, and explicit decision statuses. A reviewer who can't open the file doesn't review it.

  * A season is dozens of styles sitting at different rounds on the same day, so define your workflow statuses once at company level and keep a collection-level view alongside the per-style history.

  * Australian fashion group APG & Co, which owns Saba, Sportscraft and Jag, reported a **50% reduction in development and fit sampling costs** in FY25, with 100% of styles across the three brands on CLO and CLO-SET. Designing in 3D got them part of the way. The saving landed once reviewing, versioning, and approving moved into a shared workspace too, because physical samples became confirmations rather than experiments.




## **What Is a Digital Sample Review?**

A digital sample review is the process of evaluating and signing off on a garment sample using a shared digital record rather than email, chat, and printouts.

Two terms get mixed up here, and the distinction matters when you're choosing tools. A digital sample is the asset: a 3D garment, a set of turntable renders, or a photographed physical sample. A digital sample review is the process wrapped around that asset, covering who looks at it, what they comment on, which version they commented on, and what was decided.

You can run a digital sample review on a physical sample, and most teams do for the later rounds. The garment is real, the review is digital, and the photos, measurements, comments, and approval stay in one place.

## **Why Email-Based Sample Reviews Break Down**

A sample review produces four kinds of information at once, and email carries one of them well.

![d18ebc1764364972a7a07a016e11eb45](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202608/83bcf55202f24384b7e226f9894d1b9b/images/d18ebc1764364972a7a07a016e11eb45image.png)

**Feedback loses its anchor.** "The shoulder looks off" is unusable without a point on the garment attached to it. The reader has to reconstruct which image, which view, and which seam.

**Versions fork silently.** Every attachment is a copy. Once two people reply to different messages in the thread, there are two live versions of the truth and no way to tell which is newer.

**Decisions stay implied.** Threads end when people stop replying, not when someone decides. Weeks later, "was that approved?" has no answer except somebody's memory.

**Vendors see fragments.** The factory gets whatever was forwarded, rarely the full picture and never the version history. They fill the gaps with assumptions, and the assumptions show up in the next sample.

The expensive part of all this is the extra round that gets triggered when a review ends ambiguously.

## **The Sample Review Workflow, Step by Step**

![9bddf565ddbd4d30b62954e3ef3023cd](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202608/83bcf55202f24384b7e226f9894d1b9b/images/9bddf565ddbd4d30b62954e3ef3023cdimage.png)

### **Step 1: Name the Round and What It Decides**

Most review confusion comes from running one generic "sample review" for four different purposes. Each round answers a different question, and mixing them re-opens settled decisions.

  * Proto, or first sample, decides whether the concept and silhouette are right. It does not decide graded measurements or final trims.

  * Fit sample decides whether the base-size measurements and balance work on body. It does not decide whether the factory can produce the style at volume.

  * Pre-production sample, or PP sample, decides whether this factory can build the garment correctly in the approved materials. It does not decide design direction, which is locked by this point.

  * Top of production, or TOP, decides whether bulk output matches the approved PP sample. It does not decide anything about the design or the fit.




Write the round type on the review itself. It sets the scope of acceptable feedback, which is the cheapest way to stop a merchandiser from re-opening a neckline during a PP review.

![5d22f6a76d58477eb9f6c37f6427ae6b](https://storagefiles.clo-set.com/public/community/202608/83bcf55202f24384b7e226f9894d1b9b/images/5d22f6a76d58477eb9f6c37f6427ae6bimage.png)

### **Step 2: Upload Each Round as a New Version of the Same Style**

Everyone needs to be able to open the sample, and everyone needs to know which round they're looking at.

The reviewer who blocks your round is usually the one who can't open the file. If reviewing a garment needs a license, a plugin, or a 400 MB download, some share of your reviewers will substitute a screenshot and comment on that instead. The working standard is a browser-viewable link: click, rotate, zoom into a seam, comment, with nothing installed and no copy of your editable file in circulation.

Versioning is the other half. Each round should be uploaded as a new version of the same record, not as a new file with a new name. In CLO-SET that record is a Style inside a Room, and CLO or Marvelous Designer users can push a ZPRJ or ZPAC straight into it with Direct Upload. Because the version sits on the Style, last week's shared link still resolves, earlier rounds stay readable, and nobody maintains a file-naming convention to know what's current. (If your 3D assets are still spread across drives and inboxes, fix that first: [how to manage and share 3D garment files](https://style.clo-set.com/en/resources/article/e4676767464541a5b94f57e11082ee2c).)

### **Step 3: Pin Feedback to the Garment, Not the Thread**

A comment attached to a specific point on a specific version is self-explaining a month later. The same comment in an email is not.

Spatially pinned notes and threaded discussion do different jobs, and you want both. Pinned notes mark the exact point in 3D that needs to change. Threaded discussion carries the reasoning and the attachments. In CLO-SET these are Annotation and Comment, and 3D annotations export to PDF when a factory wants the markup alongside the spec.

Keep one issue per note, because a note containing four problems gets partially fixed and fully closed. State the correction, not just the observation: "shoulder point 1 cm too wide, take from the sleeve head" is actionable, while "shoulder looks off" starts another round of questions. And comment on the version you were shown, so old notes stay attached to the round they described.

### **Step 4: Change the Workflow Status Explicitly**

Every round closes with a recorded status, an owner, and a date. Three cover most teams.

**Approved.** Proceed. Nothing further is expected on this round.

**Approved with conditions.** Proceed, but named corrections must appear in the next version. List them somewhere structural, because in the comment stream they get read once and forgotten.

**Revise.** A new version is required before moving on.

Use whatever vocabulary suits your calendar. What makes it a record is that the status sits on the style and changes deliberately when someone decides.

CLO-SET splits this into two fields, worth knowing before you set it up. Workflow Status is the development stage and sits on the style itself. Each colorway inside that style carries its own Status, so a style can be at one stage overall while individual colorways sit at different points. Both sets of names are yours to define in Company Settings, so "proto review" and "PP approved" mean the same thing to everyone using them. Workflow Status can be changed on several styles at once from the Workroom, and it is the field the search filter and the Line Sheet read from.

Name one decision owner per round. Skip that and you get the most expensive mistake in sampling: two functions each believing the other approved something.

### **Step 5: Update the Tech Pack on Every Round, Not Only the Last One**

The tech pack is easy to mistake for a final deliverable that gets built once and sent to the factory. Treating it that way is where spec drift comes from.

Every round produces corrections, and the factory works from the specification, not from your review notes. A measurement change agreed in a fit review and never written into the spec reappears as a defect two rounds later. So the tech pack gets updated in the pass that closes each round, not at the end.

This is much easier when the garment data and the document come from the same source, which is the case when the spec is built on the same record the review ran on. The clearest version of that: [generating a tech pack directly from the 3D garment](https://style.clo-set.com/en/resources/article/4c680edb7dd0417fb49086d0e812a74a). Building the format from scratch? There's a [free production-ready tech pack template](https://style.clo-set.com/en/resources/article/ea95bf7b27ca48619b9b76752097aa70).

### **Step 6: Close the Round, Then Either Open the Next Version or Release the Style**

Leaving a round open is how comment streams turn into archaeology. Close it: change the workflow status, confirm the corrections reached the spec, note who decided.

From there a round has exactly two exits. Either the style needs another version, so you open the next round against the new upload and the loop runs again, or the style is approved for production and the current tech pack goes to the factory. Most styles go around two or three times before taking the second exit.

Closed rounds stay readable as a record of when each decision was made and on what basis. That's what you need the next time a vendor and a buyer remember the same meeting differently.

## **Running This Across a Collection, Not One Style at a Time**

Everything above describes one style. A season is a hundred of them at different rounds on the same day, and the problem changes shape at that scale. The question is no longer which version is current. It is which of these forty styles is blocked, and on whom.

**Per style,** you want the round history, the current Workflow Status, the Status on each colorway, and the open corrections.

**Across the collection,** you want every style in the line with its current status, so you can see what's waiting on a decision without opening forty records. This is what CLO-SET's Assortment is for: a Room built for reviewing and deciding on multiple Styles at once. Filtering the line by Workflow Status answers the merchandiser's real question, which is what is still unapproved with six weeks to go.

So define your Workflow Status names once, at company level, before the season starts. Stages invented per style don't aggregate. While you're in there, set the leadtime end status, which is what lets the platform measure how long each stage takes.

## **Who Should Be in a Sample Review, and What They Decide**

Reviews get slow when everyone comments on everything. Assigning decision rights by function works better than shortening the invite list.

  * Designer decides silhouette, proportion, color, and graphic placement, and should not block graded measurements or construction method.

  * Technical designer or patternmaker decides fit, measurements, balance, and construction, and should not block commercial calls.

  * Merchandiser decides whether the style still fits the range and the price, and should not block technical corrections.

  * Production and sourcing decides feasibility, materials availability, and cost impact, and should not block design intent.

  * Vendor or factory identifies what is buildable and where they need clarification. A factory never approves its own sample.

  * Buyer, where one is involved, decides range sign-off and should not block individual construction details.




## **How Many Sample Rounds Should a Style Take?**

Three physical rounds (proto, fit, PP) is the common baseline for a style with no unusual construction. Teams that pre-review in 3D routinely get one of those back, because proportion, colorway, and graphic placement get settled before anything is cut. Which rounds 3D can take and which still need fabric in your hands is a longer answer.

Your own trend is the number to watch. Rounds per style, averaged across a season, tells you whether the process is converging or just generating traffic.

## **What to Look for in Sample Review Software**

Judge tools against the failure modes above, not against a feature list. Eight things matter: a browser viewer that needs no license, feedback pinned to a point on the garment alongside threaded discussion, versioning on the record instead of in file names, configurable decision statuses, a collection-level view, workspace-level access control, a connection to product data, and external access that doesn't cost a seat.

On where it lives: if you already run a PLM, sample review sits alongside it, not inside it, because PLM is strong at records and weak at visual review. Still deciding whether you need one? We compared the options here: [Do you need a fashion PLM? 8 product development tools compared](https://style.clo-set.com/en/resources/article/d3a24e2976254e4ab816812436a4e780).

## **How CLO-SET Handles This**

CLO-SET is a cloud workspace built for this workflow, organised as Spaces, Rooms, and Styles so a season has somewhere to live. The six steps above map onto it directly: Direct Upload from CLO for each new version, a browser-based 3D Viewer so vendors review without a license, Annotation and Comment for the two kinds of feedback, Workflow Status and Status for decisions, Permission for access at Space, Room, or Style level, and Assortment for the collection view. On the documentation side, the Web Tech Pack carries the spec into production: Measurement tracks 2D and 3D measurements from CLO against target measurements, Bill of Materials holds the components, and Construction and Cost Estimation complete the document the factory works from.

The clearest evidence at scale comes from APG & Co, the Australian group behind Saba, Sportscraft and Jag. In FY25 the group reported a **50% reduction in development and fit sampling costs** , because physical samples became confirmations rather than experiments, and an **80% time reduction on print strike-offs** , with prints, colours, and placement finalised digitally before anything was printed. By then **100% of styles** across all three brands were developed and managed on CLO and CLO-SET, and **10 supplier factories** had been trained and onboarded, covering half the group's woven factories.

Two things to be precise about. Those numbers come from CLO and CLO-SET used together, not from either alone: CLO is where garments are designed and simulated, CLO-SET is where they get reviewed, versioned, approved, and handed off, and a team using design software on its own still exports static tech packs and emails them out. And these are eighth-year figures. APG & Co adopted CLO in 2019, the savings compounded as adoption spread into the supply chain, and the results were assessed externally rather than self-reported: the Australian Fashion Industry Awards named the group a Best Use of Technology finalist for 2026. [Read the full story](https://style.clo-set.com/en/resources/article/d15a2cda1cbe4398b2f2fa89601761e4), or the underlying report in [Ragtrader](https://www.ragtrader.com.au/news/afia-finalists-2026-best-use-of-technology).

**[**[**Try CLO-SET for free**](https://style.clo-set.com/aboutus)**]**

## **FAQ**

**What is the difference between a digital sample and a digital sample review?**

A digital sample is the asset: a 3D garment or a photographed physical sample. A digital sample review is the process around it, covering who comments, on which version, and what gets decided. A team can own plenty of digital samples and still run analog reviews over email, which is where most of the lost time sits.

**How do you run a sample review with a factory that has no 3D software?**

Share a link to a browser-based 3D view rather than the project file. The factory rotates and zooms the garment in any browser, and comments land on the garment instead of in a separate email chain. This is also the safer route, since they never receive an editable copy of your file.

**Should sample review live in the PLM or in a separate tool?**

PLM is built to hold records: BOMs, specs, costing, approvals as data. Visual review is a different job, involving large 3D assets, spatial comments, fast version turnover, and external participants who will never have a PLM seat. Most teams run visual review in a tool built for it and let the approved output feed the PLM record.

**How do you keep an auditable record of who approved what?**

Three things have to be captured together: the version reviewed, the decision, and the person who made it, with a timestamp. If any one of those is missing, the record won't settle a dispute. Platforms with per-asset version history and explicit workflow statuses capture all three without anyone maintaining a spreadsheet.

**How do you manage sample reviews across a whole collection?**

Define your workflow statuses once at company level so every style uses the same vocabulary, then keep two views: the round history per style, and a line-level view showing every style with its current status. At season scale the question is no longer which version is current. It becomes which of these forty styles is blocked and on whom, and only a collection view answers that. In CLO-SET this is Assortment, a Room for reviewing and deciding on multiple styles at once.

**Do you need CLO as well as CLO-SET?**

They do different halves of the job. CLO is the 3D garment simulation software where garments are designed, patterned, and simulated. CLO-SET is the connected workspace where those assets are reviewed, versioned, approved, and handed off to teams and suppliers. Design software on its own still ends with someone exporting a static tech pack and emailing it, which reintroduces the ambiguity 3D was supposed to remove. The published savings at APG & Co came from running both.

**How many people should be in a sample review?**

Fewer commenters than you think, with clearer decision rights. Reviews slow down because six people comment on everything, not because too few were invited. Assign each function a scope, such as fit to the technical designer and range fit to the merchandiser, and treat comments outside that scope as notes rather than blockers.

**How much does 3D garment simulation actually save a fashion business?** For Australian fashion group APG & Co — the company behind Saba, Sportscraft and Jag — the answer in FY25 was a 50% reduction in development and fit sampling costs and an 80% time reduction on print strike-offs, with 100% of styles across all three brands developed and managed on CLO and CLO-SET. Those results earned APG & Co a finalist spot for [Best Use of Technology at the 2026 Australian Fashion Industry Awards](https://www.ragtrader.com.au/news/afia-finalists-2026-best-use-of-technology).

The numbers are impressive. But the more useful story for any brand evaluating digital product creation is _where_ those numbers came from — because they didn’t come from design software alone.

## **What results can a brand expect from 3D garment simulation?**

APG & Co’s FY25 results, as reported by industry publication Ragtrader, break down like this:

  * APG & Co developed and managed **100% of styles** across Saba, Sportscraft and Jag on the CLO and CLO-SET platform.

  * Print strike-offs became **80% faster** because prints, colours and placement were finalised digitally before anything was printed.

  * Development and fit sampling costs fell by **50%** , because physical samples became confirmations rather than experiments.

  * **10 supplier factories** were fully trained and onboarded on CLO and CLO-SET, covering half of the group’s woven factories.




One caveat that matters: these are eighth-year numbers. APG & Co adopted CLO in 2019 as the first Australian fashion retailer to do so. The savings compounded as adoption spread — first through design teams, then through the supply chain. Over this eight-year journey, APG’s GM of Supply Chain and Head of Global Quality have been valuable partners in pushing the boundaries of 3D adoption. Their passion for improving fit, quality, and sustainability as a standard for fashion companies and supplier factories provided invaluable industry feedback, helping shape how CLO-SET delivers impactful agility and efficiencies today.

  


## **Why the True Synergy Happens When 3D Design Meets a Collaborative Platform?**

While 3D design software is a powerful tool on its own, its true potential is unlocked when it works in synergy with a connected collaboration platform. When 3D tools are used independently, digitally simulated garments are often exported as static tech packs and emailed to partners, bringing back the ambiguity that 3D was supposed to eliminate. Fit comments get scattered across email threads, and physical strike-offs are still couriered back and forth. The real breakthrough happens when 3D design is seamlessly integrated with a collaborative workspace.

This synergy creates mutual savings across the entire supply chain, extending far beyond any single company's success. Whether it’s the brand’s internal team creating the 3D assets or the vendor factories driving the 3D design, a shared workspace aligns everyone involved. When both brands and suppliers can open, review, and interact with the exact same 3D garment in real time, version confusion disappears.

Designing in 3D is an exceptional capability, but the most significant ROI—drastically reduced sampling costs and strike-off times—is mutually shared when reviewing, versioning, and approving happen natively in a shared 3D environment across the entire supply chain.

  


## **How do you onboard suppliers to a 3D workflow?**

APG & Co’s supplier strategy had three moves worth borrowing:

**Remove the cost barrier first.** APG & Co initially covered its suppliers’ CLO-SET licence fees to accelerate adoption. Funding supplier licences looks like an expense; in practice it’s the cheapest way to eliminate thousands of hours of email-and-courier iteration.

**Sequence by brand, not big-bang.** Saba completed 100% of development styles on CLO in 2022. Sportscraft and Jag followed in 2023. Each rollout de-risked and informed the next, and by 2025 ten supplier factories were fully onboarded.

**Make it the industry standard, not a secret.** In 2026, APG & Co introduced the platform to industry body Seamless, which has since onboarded it as a supporter and promotes it to all members.

## **How long does it take to see ROI on digital product creation?**

APG & Co’s timeline offers a realistic benchmark:

Year / Milestone

2019 First CLO adoption : the first Australian fashion retailer to do so

2020–21 : Remote collaborative design through COVID accelerated adoption

2022 : Saba reaches 100% of development styles on CLO

2023 : Sportscraft and Jag reach full development on CLO

2025 : 10 supplier factories fully onboarded on CLO and CLO-SET

FY25 : 50% sampling cost reduction; 80% faster strike-offs; 100% of styles managed on platform

The early wins (fewer samples, faster iteration) arrive within the first seasons. The transformational numbers arrived when supply-chain adoption crossed critical mass — a useful expectation-setter for any brand building a business case.

## **Third-party validation: AFIA 2026 finalist**

Results self-reported by vendors are easy to discount. APG & Co’s outcomes were assessed by the Australian Fashion Industry Awards, which named the group a **Best Use of Technology finalist for 2026** , calling its journey an industry best-practice case study in digitising Australian fashion development. Winners are announced 6 August 2026 in Melbourne — congratulations to the entire APG & Co team, and we’ll be cheering. 🎉

## **Frequently asked questions**

**What is the ROI of 3D garment simulation?**   
Results vary by adoption depth. APG & Co reported a 50% reduction in development and fit sampling costs and an 80% time reduction on print strike-offs in FY25, after reaching 100% platform adoption across three brands and onboarding 10 supplier factories.

  
**How long does it take to fully adopt 3D garment simulation?**

The timeline varies significantly depending on a brand's scale, internal strategy, and supplier network. While initial wins—such as reduced physical sampling—often appear within the first few seasons, full supply-chain integration is typically a multi-year journey. As a real-world benchmark, APG & Co took roughly three years to bring its first brand (Saba) to 100% 3D development, and about six years to reach full adoption across its three brands and entire vendor network.

**What’s the difference between CLO and CLO-SET?**

CLO is the 3D garment simulation software where garments are designed and simulated. CLO-SET is the connected collaboration platform where those 3D assets are reviewed, versioned, approved and handed off across teams and suppliers — the layer where supply-chain-wide savings occur.

**What is a digital strike-off?**

A digital strike-off finalises prints, colours and placement on a simulated 3D garment before physical printing. APG & Co reported this cut strike-off time by 80% compared with physical rounds.
